subChunks.title: Working with Archives, Repositories & Archivists

storyBeats.txt: Online records are extraordinary — but they are a curated fraction of what survives, Theodora said. The rest is in boxes. On shelves. In repositories that require you to show up, follow rules, and engage with human beings.

Archivists are not obstacles. They are specialists with intimate knowledge of their collections. A two-minute conversation with the right archivist has saved researchers months of misdirected searching. Treat them as colleagues, not service workers.

And when you do go online — when you consult an archivist's finding aid or request a digitised image — remember that what you are seeing is the product of years of conservation, cataloguing, and often underfunded care. The infrastructure of memory is not free.

subChunks.hookHtml:
Digital genealogy has created the impression that most historical records can be found by typing a name into a search box. For a significant proportion of the genealogical record, this is now true. But the most valuable, most specialised, and most unique records — uncatalogued family collections, unpublished estate papers, specialist ecclesiastical archives, manuscript repositories, military regimental records — remain accessible only by visiting an archive, understanding its systems, and working directly with its staff.

Professional genealogical research requires fluency in archival working practices: how repositories are organised; how finding aids function; how to order and handle documents; how to make the most of an archivist's expertise; and how to manage a research visit productively. These skills are not taught by search boxes.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Types of Repositories

Genealogical records are held across a wide range of repository types:

  • National archives: TNA (Kew), National Records of Scotland (Edinburgh), PRONI (Belfast), National Archives of Ireland (Dublin), Library of Congress, NARA (United States). Hold government-created records.
  • County record offices (CROs): Hold parish registers, quarter sessions records, estate papers, and local government records for their county area. In England and Wales, the primary repository for most genealogical records.
  • Diocesan record offices: Hold Church of England parish registers not transferred to CROs, bishops' registers, and other ecclesiastical records. Sometimes co-located with CROs.
  • University libraries and special collections: Hold manuscript collections, estate papers deposited by landowners, and unique research materials not available elsewhere.
  • Local studies libraries: Hold printed local history collections, directories, local newspapers, and sometimes microfilm collections of parish registers.
  • Private archives: Estate papers held by solicitors, landed families, or businesses. Access requires negotiation with the owner; the Manorial Documents Register and the National Register of Archives (NRA, now part of TNA's Discovery database) identify many private holdings.

Finding Aids and Catalogues

A finding aid is any tool that helps a researcher locate records within an archive. Types include: repository-level catalogues (listing all holdings by collection and series); collection-level lists (describing the contents of a specific fonds or deposit); item-level catalogues (describing individual documents); and indexes (name, place, or subject indexes to specific record series).

Key national catalogues: TNA's Discovery (discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk) searches records held at TNA and descriptions of records held by hundreds of other repositories; it is the single most important online finding aid for English genealogical research. Archives Wales (archiveswales.org.uk) covers Welsh repositories. ScotlandsPeople and NRS indexes cover Scottish statutory records. PRONI's e-catalogue covers Northern Irish holdings.

Ordering Documents

Most archives require advance registration. Documents must be ordered from finding aids before visiting — most archives have a limited number of production slots and do not permit browsing in the stacks. Key practices:

  • Order in advance: TNA documents must be ordered online up to 3 days in advance; many CROs require booking appointments and specifying documents in advance.
  • Photography rules: Most archives now permit personal photography (without flash) of most documents. Some records have restrictions (copyright, conservation, data protection). Always check in advance and follow the archivist's instructions.
  • Handling rules: Pencils only (no pens); clean hands; do not lean on documents; follow the archive's prescribed handling method for fragile materials. Document boxes are loaded and unloaded by the researcher, not staff, in most repositories.
  • Document reference system: Every document has a reference number (e.g., TNA reference E 179/253/12). Record this precisely — it is the basis of your citation and enables you or another researcher to locate the same document again.

Working with Archivists

Archivists have deep knowledge of their collections' content and structure, the records that were created, and what has survived. They are not genealogists — they will not search on your behalf — but they can advise on: which record series is most likely to contain what you seek; what related collections exist; whether finding aids are complete (some collections are inadequately catalogued); and whether records are restricted or need special handling.

Effective archivist engagement: prepare a precise written question before approaching them; describe your research question, what you have already found, and what you are looking for; use correct terminology for record types. Do not ask open-ended questions ('can you help me find my family?'); ask targeted ones ('I am looking for settlement examination records for this parish in this period — do you hold them and where are they catalogued?').

Remote Research and Document Supply

Not all research can be conducted in person. Most repositories offer: document photography on request (fees apply); digital image supply for accessible records; and microfilm reader provision (for records held on microfilm). The Society of Genealogists (London) holds the largest publicly accessible genealogical library in the UK and provides research services for non-members by correspondence.

Research agents (professional researchers based in specific repositories or regions) can conduct repository visits on behalf of remote clients. The Association of Professional Genealogists and AGRA both maintain directories of agents by geographic specialism.

International Archives

International archives each have their own systems, languages, access conditions, and cataloguing practices. Key contacts: PARES (Spain and Spanish colonial archives, pares.mcu.es); ANOM (French colonial archives, anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr); Family History Library in Salt Lake City (the world's largest genealogical library, with microfilm collections from 110 countries and online FamilySearch integration); and the IFHF (International Federation of Family History Societies) directory of national genealogical societies.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what an archive is, why not all historical records are online, and what you need to do before visiting an archive to research your family history.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: You need to research a family who lived in Derbyshire in the 1700s. You believe they held copyhold land under a local manor, and you want to find any surviving manorial court rolls. Describe the steps you would take to: (a) identify whether any court rolls survive for the relevant manor; (b) identify which repository holds them; (c) prepare for a research visit to that repository; and (d) make the most effective use of your time there.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(a) To identify whether any court rolls survive: use the TNA's Manorial Documents Register (MDR), available online at manorial.nationalarchives.gov.uk. Search for the specific manor or all manors in the relevant township. The MDR records whether court rolls are known to survive and where they are held.

(b) The MDR result will show the repository — most likely Derbyshire Record Office (Matlock) for county manors, but possibly TNA (for royal or ecclesiastical manors), a university library, or a private solicitor's collection. For private holdings, the NRA/Discovery database at TNA may provide more detail on access conditions.

(c) Preparation for the visit: Contact the repository to register as a reader (most require advance registration with ID proof). Identify the specific document references for the court rolls from the finding aid or from the MDR entry. Book a document production slot (most repositories require advance ordering). Check photography policy. Review basic Latin palaeography if the rolls are pre-1733 (when Latin became mandatory in English courts — ironic for manorial records which were already using English by that point). Note: manorial court rolls often use abbreviated Latin formulas even for post-1538 entries; prepare standard formulaic phrases.

(d) During the visit: Use pencil only. Photograph all relevant entries (name searches, not just confirmed matches). Record all document references precisely. Ask the archivist at the start if there are finding aids or indexes to the specific roll series — some repositories have internal name indexes not visible in the online catalogue. If you find gaps in the series (years with no rolls), ask whether they are lost or simply not yet transferred; they may be with a local solicitor or private estate.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: You are researching a Devon family and have identified that their estate papers (including correspondence, accounts, and a potential family bible) were deposited with a local solicitor in the 1960s. The solicitor's firm no longer exists. The National Register of Archives shows a deposit was made but gives no current location. What steps would you take to locate these records, and what challenges might you encounter?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Locating records that have passed through a dissolved solicitors' firm requires tracing the firm's succession. Steps: (1) Search the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA) register for the firm's history — when it dissolved, whether it was taken over by another firm or wound up. A successor firm may have taken custody of stored client papers. (2) Contact Devon Record Office (DRO): solicitor-deposited papers are often transferred to county record offices when firms dissolve, particularly if the depositing party (the estate or family) has also dissolved or cannot be contacted. DRO may have received this deposit and not yet fully catalogued it — NRA descriptions are frequently incomplete. (3) Contact the National Archives (TNA Discovery) to update the NRA entry — TNA may be able to advise on whether a notification of transfer was received. (4) Contact Devon Family History Society: local societies often have knowledge of private collections that are not formally recorded anywhere. (5) Contact the local estate, if still extant: the depositing family may have retained other papers or know where the solicitor's collection went.

Challenges: Dissolved firm records may have been destroyed under records retention guidelines (most legal documents have a maximum retention period; after that they may have been shredded). The deposit may be with a successor firm that has not informed NRA of its current location. The family bible — if it survived — is a private document and may have passed into family hands rather than remaining with the solicitor's collection. Even if located, access to private papers requires permission from the current owner (which may be the former client family if they are still identifiable). If access is granted, the researcher must follow any conditions the owner sets. These challenges are common in private archive research and require persistence and local knowledge.
learningObjectives: Identify the main types of repositories holding genealogical records and the categories of records each typically holds.
Use TNA's Discovery catalogue and equivalent national finding aids to locate records at TNA and in other repositories.
Describe the practical requirements for visiting an archive: registration, advance ordering, handling rules, and photography policies.
Explain how to engage effectively with archivists and make best use of their expertise.
commonMistakes: Assuming that records not visible in online catalogues do not exist — many collections are inadequately catalogued or held in private hands not listed online.
Arriving at an archive without pre-ordering documents — most repositories have strict production systems and will not retrieve documents for unscheduled visitors.
Using a pen in an archive — pencils only is a near-universal rule; pens risk irreparable damage to documents.
Failing to record precise document references (series, piece, folio) at the time of research, making citation and re-location impossible.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly identifies the range of repository types and the record categories each holds.
Demonstrates knowledge of TNA Discovery and how it covers both TNA holdings and other repositories.
Describes a realistic and correctly sequenced archive visit preparation process.
Shows understanding of how to engage productively with archivists through precise, targeted questions.

questions.questionHtml: What is TNA's Discovery catalogue and what scope does it cover?
options: A catalogue of all genealogical records digitised by TNA, covering only records held at Kew
An online catalogue searching TNA's own holdings and record descriptions from hundreds of other UK repositories
A subscription database for genealogical DNA matching
A catalogue of all English and Welsh parish registers from 1538 onwards
questions.correctAnswer: An online catalogue searching TNA's own holdings and record descriptions from hundreds of other UK repositories
questions.explanationHtml: Discovery is TNA's catalogue at discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk. It covers TNA's own holdings (the former Public Record Office collections) and also holds record descriptions from hundreds of other archives — county record offices, university libraries, private collections — making it the most important single starting point for locating English genealogical records.

questions.questionHtml: You are planning a first visit to a county record office to consult a 19th-century estate collection. What should you do before arriving?
options: Arrive when the office opens and ask the archivist to suggest what to look at
Register as a reader in advance, identify the specific document references from the finding aid, pre-order the boxes, and confirm the photography policy
Bring a credit card to pay for document access
Check that the collection is fully digitised and available on FindMyPast before visiting
questions.correctAnswer: Register as a reader in advance, identify the specific document references from the finding aid, pre-order the boxes, and confirm the photography policy
questions.explanationHtml: Most county record offices require advance reader registration (with ID). Documents must be ordered in advance from finding aids — production slots are limited. Photography policies vary and must be confirmed before the visit. Arriving without preparation wastes visit time and may result in not being able to see the records at all.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher cannot find a record they expect to exist in an archive's online catalogue. What is the most professionally sound conclusion?
options: The record does not exist and the research should move on
The archive has lost the record
Online catalogues are incomplete — the record may exist but be uncatalogued, miscatalogued, or held in a private collection not listed online; direct contact with the archivist is the next step
The researcher has the wrong archive
questions.correctAnswer: Online catalogues are incomplete — the record may exist but be uncatalogued, miscatalogued, or held in a private collection not listed online; direct contact with the archivist is the next step
questions.explanationHtml: Many collections are inadequately catalogued in online systems. Archivists often have knowledge of holdings not visible in the online catalogue. Private collections may be listed only in NRA (Discovery) or not at all. Treating absence from an online catalogue as absence of the record is a significant methodological error.
